items.name: Thermal socks
items.fact: Trench foot needs only about ten hours of wet at temperatures as mild as 55 degrees; a dry foot restarts that count.

items.name: Rain ponchos
items.fact: We get rain three out of five days in the PNW from November through February, and clothes that stay wet cost a body up to 40 percent more heat, enough for hypothermia at temperatures in the forties or fifties depending on the wind.

items.name: Beanies
items.fact: Hands and feet get shut down to keep the core warm; the head never does. A cover for the scalp and ears maintains both comfort and heat for the rest of the body.

items.name: Bivvies
items.fact: A mylar sack stops about 80 percent of the heat a body radiates during sleep, and one that folds back down and fits back in the backpack makes that true night after night.

items.name: Underwear
items.fact: One of the most asked for items for any care package drive, because a spare pair is the difference between washing and going without.

items.name: Gloves
items.fact: Warm fingers hold about twice the dexterity of cold ones.

items.name: Antifungal cream
items.fact: A damp foot grows fungus in days; getting rid of it takes a month of treating it.

items.name: Barrier cream
items.fact: Zinc oxide has been recognized by the FDA as a skin protectant against wind and cold. Reducing skin breakage is one of the only ways to prevent infections.

items.name: Wet wipes
items.fact: A moist towel can remove two thirds of dirt and grime in moments where running water is not in reach.

items.name: Toothbrushes
items.fact: Mechanical brushing is the only proven method to remove everything growing on teeth.

items.name: Toothbrush cases
items.fact: Stored anywhere, a barrier keeps dirt off bristles and anything on them off anything important.
